blindSummary:
This state/province sits squarely in the geography of the former racially-segregated homelands, where traditional-courts jurisdiction is most extensive following the segregation-era map: an international human-rights organisation's analysis of the 2019 traditional-leadership act identifies these areas as a separate legal system whose adjudication of gender and sexual matters under customary law with a consent presumption against the individual constitutes the principal sub-national legal divergence in the country. The act was declared invalid by a national high court in 2023 but suspended and extended; the replacement bill has been delayed. No state/province has religious criminal law; no statute criminalises a visitor's expression here.

This state/province is also one of only three jurisdictions in the country with its own representative hate-crime prevalence study (2010, noted in an LGBT-rights NGO's review alongside the two metropolitan states/provinces), giving it a data-presence signal: incidents against queer people here are, historically, more likely to appear in research than only in the dark figure of unreported crime that characterises most states/provinces. No trans-specific incident series was found. The 2010 study covers gay and lesbian people; its relevance to a trans visitor is as a proxy for reporting culture and the volume of anti-queer violence in a traditional-authority-heavy state/province.

Local risk sits slightly below the country-wide average. Against the sister former-homeland state/province, the two share the customary-authority finding at similar magnitude; this state/province's additional 2010 data presence does not raise it above the sister because the study documents violence prevalence rather than institutional response capacity. Against a coastal state/province, this one is judged better placed because the coastal adds a retrieved township queerphobia study and the official alignment of a major ethnic monarch and an ethnic-leader confederation against queer people, while this state/province has the jurisdictional risk without a comparable named-authority statement. Against the metropolitan states/provinces, the gap reflects metro institutional functioning versus rural customary-authority geography. The under-reporting caveat applies equally: a state/province with more recorded hate crime may simply have better reporting rather than more danger.
